beats.text: What if the OS could take the CPU back in the middle of a burst? That is preemptive scheduling.
S R T F, shortest remaining time first, is the preemptive version of S J F. Now the processes arrive at different times.
P one starts at zero, with eight to do. At one, P two arrives, needing four.
P one still has seven left. Four is less. So P two takes the CPU.
P three and P four arrive, but neither beats what P two has left. Then P four, P one, and P three.
Average waiting time: six point five.
Round robin is first come, first served, plus a timer. Each process runs for at most one time quantum, Q. Then it goes to the back of the queue.
Back to twenty-four, three and three, with a quantum of four. P one runs four, and the timer sends it back.
P two and P three finish inside their turns. Then P one runs alone, all the way to thirty.
Waiting times six, four and seven. Seventeen over three is about five point six seven.
The slide prints five point three. That is an arithmetic slip, so always check your own division.
The quantum decides everything. Make it huge, and round robin turns into first come, first served.
Make it tiny, and the CPU spends its time switching. The quantum must be much larger than a context switch.
Priority scheduling gives the CPU to the highest priority. The smallest number is the highest.
Priorities three, one, four, five and two give the order P two, P five, P one, P three, P four. Average wait, eight point two.
But a low priority process can wait forever while higher ones keep arriving. That is starvation.
The cure is aging. The longer a process waits, the higher its priority grows, until it gets its turn.
For the exam.
S R T F preempts when a shorter job arrives.
Round robin: one quantum, then the back of the queue.
A huge quantum becomes FCFS.
Priority: the smallest number runs first.
Starvation is cured by aging.
